entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Qing Dynasty (清朝, Qīng Cháo), founded in 1644 when the Manchu Aisin Gioro clan conquered China from the north replacing the Ming Dynasty — was China's last imperial dynasty, ruling approximately 400-500 million people at its height across the largest Chinese empire ever assembled (including Xinjiang, Tibet, Mongolia, and Taiwan), and ending in 1912 when Emperor Puyi abdicated following the Xinhai Revolution, closing 2,132 years of Chinese imperial rule.

The Qing rulers were ethnic Manchus — a small northeastern people who conquered the vastly more numerous Han Chinese — and the dynasty's management of this demographic asymmetry was one of history's most sophisticated strategies of minority rule: Manchu banners maintained military control while Han Chinese were incorporated into governance through the civil service examination system; Qing emperors presented themselves as universal rulers to different subjects (Confucian Son of Heaven to Han Chinese, Khan to Mongols, Patron of Tibetan Buddhism to Tibetans), creating a multi-ethnic imperial synthesis.

Qing's decline and fall is one of history's most consequential collapses: the Opium Wars (1839-1842, 1856-1860) opened China to Western commercial dominance; the Taiping Rebellion (1850-1864, approximately 20-30 million dead — possibly history's deadliest civil war) nearly destroyed the dynasty; the 1895 Sino-Japanese War lost Taiwan and revealed Qing weakness; the Boxer Rebellion (1900) led to humiliating Western occupation of Beijing. The 1911 Xinhai Revolution ended 2,000 years of imperial governance, creating the Republic of China.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Qing Dynasty — China's last imperial dynasty ruling 400-500 million people, assembling China's largest empire, whose collapse ended 2,132 years of imperial rule — is one of history's most consequential ruling houses, whose fall created modern China's political and territorial foundations.
